## Simple explanation

Interpolation estimates a value between points that are already known. If
measurements show a system's temperature at 10:00 and 10:10, interpolation
can estimate its temperature at 10:05.

## Technical explanation

An interpolation method constructs an estimate within the range of supplied
data points. Linear interpolation connects neighboring points with a straight
line; spline methods use piecewise polynomials for a smoother curve. The
choice of method imposes assumptions about how values change between
observations.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Interpolation appears in resampling signals and images, aligning time
series, and filling gaps in measurements. The method can affect downstream
features and predictions, so engineers should preserve missingness
information and avoid using future data when constructing time-dependent
features.

## How it works

For two known points $(x_0,y_0)$ and $(x_1,y_1)$, linear interpolation at
$x$ between them is

$$
y(x)=y_0+\frac{x-x_0}{x_1-x_0}(y_1-y_0).
$$

This assumes a linear change between the endpoints. Extrapolation estimates
outside the known range and can be much less reliable.

## Practical example

A sensor records a value of 20 at one minute and 24 at the next. Linear
interpolation estimates 22 halfway between those measurements. For real
sensor data, the engineer should consider whether a linear trend is
reasonable and whether the gap itself signals a fault.

## Common misconceptions

- Interpolation estimates within the observed range; extrapolation goes
  beyond it.
- The estimate is not necessarily a true measurement of the unobserved
  value.
- Filling a missing value before splitting data can leak information from
  evaluation data.
